Free self-esteem tools

20 short exercises on self-esteem, 2 to 10 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • Inner critic, inner ally

    Turn over cards that show what an inner critic says on one side and what an inner ally would say about the same thing on the other.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • Your strengths, chosen and ranked

    Pick the five strengths that are most truly yours from a long list, then rank them. Not the ones you wish you had; the ones people would recognize.

    Card pick · 5 min

  • How you talk to yourself

    Rate how often a set of self-talk habits has been true lately, from harsh comparisons to generous self-forgiveness.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • A letter from the kind version of you

    Write to yourself about something you are struggling with, from the perspective of someone who loves you and knows everything about you.

    Guided writing · 10 min

  • Your comparison habits

    Tick the ways you find yourself measuring against other people. Everyone compares; the question is when, with whom, and what it does to you.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • What you would tell a friend

    Describe your situation as if it were happening to a friend, then answer them. A quick way to hear how much harsher you are on yourself.

    Guided writing · 6 min

  • How you relate to your body

    Set a handful of dials about your relationship with your body: trust, care, criticism, gratitude, ease. Not about how it looks; about how you live in it.

    Dials · 4 min

  • What your worth is riding on

    Sort the conditions people attach to feeling okay about themselves by how much yours depends on each one. Worth that rides on a condition wobbles every time the condition does.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • Whose opinion counts

    Divide 100 points across the people whose opinions shape how you feel about yourself. Most people are surprised by how few points they give to their own.

    Budget · 4 min

  • Skill against credit

    Place things you do on a grid of how good you actually are at them against how much credit you give yourself. The gap between the two is where a lot of low self-esteem lives.

    Grid · 6 min

  • Build your evidence file

    The inner critic works from a very selective file. Assemble a plan for keeping the rest of the record: what counts as evidence, where it lives, when you add to it, and when you read it.

    Plan builder · 6 min

  • A week of how you rated yourself

    Each evening, rate how you felt about yourself alongside how much you got done and how much approval you received. After a few days you can see what your self-regard is actually pegged to.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • How you earn approval

    Rank the moves you use to be liked, from the one you reach for most to the one you rarely use. Everyone has a few; the top two usually started young and worked.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • When your inner critic is loudest

    Mark the times in your week when the critical voice gets going. Self-criticism keeps a schedule, and the schedule usually points to what feeds it.

    Week map · 3 min

  • Taking a compliment in

    A short, timed exercise in letting something kind land instead of batting it away. Deflecting compliments is a habit, and this is one repetition in the other direction.

    Guided exercise · 4 min

  • How much space you take up

    Rate how often you make yourself smaller than you are: in doorways, in conversations, in what you ask for. Shrinking usually starts as politeness and turns into a reflex.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Messages you grew up with

    Tick the things you were told about yourself growing up, in words or otherwise. Messages heard young tend to get mistaken for facts.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Where the bar came from

    Write your way to the standard you hold yourself to, who set it, and what happens when you reach it. A bar that moves every time you get there is not a standard.

    Guided writing · 8 min

  • What you keep apologizing for

    Choose the things you find yourself saying sorry for, out loud or in your head. Most of them are not offenses; each apology is a small admission that you were not supposed to need or be that.

    Card pick · 4 min

  • Where your confidence lives

    Set a dial for how sure of yourself you feel in each area of life. Confidence is rarely one thing; most people have a couple of high dials and judge themselves by the low ones.

    Dials · 4 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
